idiom_name: typing.Protocol port + adapter class + pure to_legacy/to_domain functions
implementation_notes: Python's duck typing means the port can be a typing.Protocol (PEP 544) owned by the domain and satisfied structurally by the adapter; the adapter is a small class holding the client, boundary data are frozen dataclasses, and translation is a pair of pure functions (to_legacy_dto/to_domain) testable without a network. What replaces the facade/adapter/translator object trio is the protocol plus those functions; a concrete ABC is worth it when you want the inheritance checked at class-definition time, and the adapter class (rather than loose functions) when the client needs lifecycle or configuration.
pitfalls: Protocols are static-only: without @runtime_checkable, isinstance() against the port fails, and nothing at run time proves the adapter implements it.
The adapter must delegate explicitly rather than __getattr__-forwarding the client, or the whole vendor API leaks through the boundary object.
Mutable DTO fields cross the seam by reference; frozen dataclasses (or explicit copies) stop the domain mutating vendor state.
Vendor exceptions carry the SDK's type: use raise ... from exc, but translate the type, or every caller learns the vendor's error taxonomy.

variants.name: Pydantic boundary models (validated DTOs)
variants.idiom_name: pydantic BaseModel + Field(alias=...) + model_validate/model_dump at the seam
variants.implementation_notes: When the seam receives untrusted or schema-less payloads, the boundary models themselves become the layer's contract: pydantic BaseModel classes declare aliases (Field(alias="order_id")), validators normalise values, and model_validate/model_validate_json parse the foreign payload into an object the domain can trust, with model_dump(by_alias=True) producing the outbound shape. Port and adapter still exist; what changes is that validation and translation collapse into the model declaration, which is why this variant costs a dependency and should never hand vendor objects straight into the domain.
pitfalls: ValidationError is not a domain error: catch it at the seam and re-raise one local type, or every caller learns pydantic's error shape.
extra="ignore" silently drops unknown upstream fields - choose ignore/forbid/allow deliberately, since each encodes a different compatibility policy.
Pydantic models are mutable by default and validate on assignment only when configured, so a shared instance can be changed by both sides.
